newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China Buddhism scales heights of economic reform.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China Buddhism scales heights of economic reform.

text.p: Buddhism has become a hot ticket for China's tourism gurus, and even the most avid devotees of one of Asia's dominant religions have seen the light.

On Putuoshan Island, one of China's four sacred mountains, tourism authorities and Buddhist bureaucrats alike are eager to ensure they are not left behind in the rush to attract the worshipful dollar.
As Visit China '97 gets into full swing, local authorities are keen to exploit Putuoshan's popularity on the prayer trail for pilgrims from all over Southeast Asia.
"Buddhism travel is becoming an important feature of the travel industry," Gao Qiang, head of the local tourism management bureau, recently told a group of foreign journalists.

In 1996, a total of 1.32 million tourists came to Putuoshan, slightly down from the 1.38 million the year before, he said, adding that more than 300,000 visitors each year come from overseas, mostly Japan and South Korea, with many from Taiwan.
The local monks, too, with the guidance of the official Buddhist Association of China, have seen the way of the future.
CHINA'S FOUR SACRED MOUNTAINS LIKE ASIA'S FOUR SMALL DRAGONS

"We here are on one of China's four sacred mountains, which we will build like the four dragons," said Shi Miaosi, the abbot of the island's important Puji Temple, referring to the dynamic emerging economies of Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore and Thailand, often called the 'four small dragons'.
Putuoshan is one of the 1,000 or so islands that make up the Zhoushan archipelago off the coast of east China's Zhejiang Province.
It is easily reached from major cities -- three hours by fast boat from Shanghai, about an hour from the nearby port of Ningbo. An airport is being built on an island nearby.

Tourism accounts for more than six percent of Zhejiang's gross domestic product. It earned 23.2 billion yuan ($2.8 billion) in 1996 from domestic travellers, up 15 percent on 1995, and $292 million from foreign travellers, up 23.7 percent on 1995.

Zhejiang tourism officials said they want to put Zhejiang and Putuoshan on the Buddhist map, and to that end last year held their first annual regional Buddhist seminar, attracting about 700 devotees from Japan and South Korea. This year's is planned for October.

Home to 4,300 people, the idyllic island has little industry and few cars. The air is clean, and for most of the year the streets are clear and the restaurants, which serve famously fresh seafood, uncrowded.
But on the major Buddhist festival days every year, up to 200,000 Buddhists from all over China and the region crowd onto the 12.5 sq-km (4.8 sq-mile) island to pray at its temples.
SACRED PUTUOSHAN ON PILGRIM TRAIL SINCE SEVENTH CENTURY
Putuoshan has been sacred since the Tang Dynasty (618-907), when legend says the Buddhist goddess Guanyin visited the island.
Each of China's four sacred mountains -- Putuoshan, Emeishan in Sichuan province, Jiuhuashan in Anhui and Wutaishan in Shanxi -- is dedicated to the worship of a different Buddhist deity.
"Here, we are dedicated to Guanyin, the Goddess of Mercy who everyone knows of," said the 88-year-old abbot Shi.
"Local people believe she (Guanyin) actually became a goddess on another island near here called Lojiashan, and then came to Putuoshan to make it a holy and prosperous place," he said.
"We are her devoted servants and she mas made this a very prosperous Buddhist place," he said.

Clad in the flowing yellow cotton robes of his station, a small square hat on his bald head, the monk told the history of the temple and the fortunes of Buddhism since the revolution of 1949 swept in an atheistic communist government.

Flanked by pictures of visiting Communist Party dignitaries, including President Jiang Zemin, and speaking through a younger monk, Shi said Putuoshan's fortunes had waxed and waned over the centuries, peaking before the anti-Japanese war of the 1930s.

"Then we had three big temples, 88 convents, 128 small temples," he said. "At that time, any building you saw here was a temple, and any person you saw walking on the street was either a nun or a monk."
COMMUNIST TAKEOVER CHANGED FACE OF CHINESE BUDDHISM

The communist takeover changed things, he said, without elaborating on the impact of the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution that saw the wholesale destruction of many places of worship throughout China and the persecution of religious devotees.
Few of the temples and monasteries have survived.
Puji Temple, Shi said, has 600 monks and is run according to the lore of Buddhism and the rules of the Buddhist Association.
"According to the law, the government doesn't interfere with the administration of the temples," Shi said.
"Since the reform and opening policies (introduced in 1979), we have enjoyed open and good conditions.
"That is why I say we will make the four mountains comparable with the four dragons, because conditions are good and we can enjoy a very good religious policy," Shi said.
